items.question: How do you see the value of a platform that lets application developers avoid handling user data?
items.object: Platforms that let application developers avoid handling user data
items.answer: If I'm an application developer, if five, ten years ago data was a gold mine, it's becoming actually a liability. In Europe, for example, there's GDPR data privacy. We have California data privacy. In China, you actually need to pay data tax if you're using consumer data. This actually creates a platform where you as a developer don't need to deal with the user data. You're effectively pushing software to them. Again, you can have higher intelligent models, and you can access all of their context and memory as well in this.
quotes: If I'm an application developer, if five, ten years ago data was a gold mine, it's becoming actually a liability. In Europe, for example, there's GDPR data privacy. We have California data privacy. In China, you actually need to pay data tax if you're using consumer data. This actually creates a platform where you as a developer don't need to deal with the user data. You're effectively pushing software to them. Again, you can have higher intelligent models, and you can access all of their context and memory as well in this.

rubrics.text: The response observes that holding user data is becoming a liability for application developers rather than the asset it once was.
The response describes delivering software to users as an alternative to developers handling user data.
The response states that applications can access users’ contextual information without developers having to handle the underlying user data.

items.question: Why did Google Research appeal to you as a place to study how machines learn from text?
items.object: Google Research as a place to pursue language learning
items.answer: I joined Google Research because I saw the cat neuron paper, if folks remember that. I was like, okay, we should do that but for text and really figure out how to learn. Google was a great place to do that: lots of language, lots of compute.
quotes: I joined Google Research because I saw the cat neuron paper, if folks remember that. I was like, okay, we should do that but for text and really figure out how to learn. Google was a great place to do that: lots of language, lots of compute.

rubrics.text: The response states that Illia Polosukhin joined Google Research to pursue a text analogue of the learning demonstrated in the cat neuron paper.

items.question: How did you see the practical promise of the transformer architecture as it was emerging at Google?
items.object: The transformer architecture and its potential for practical applications
items.answer: My team was working on question answering, machine translation, and as part of that, due to even requirements and latency for google.com, we were trying to figure out how to actually build a deep learning model that can consume lots of context and really reason about it without taking a ton of time to process that. That's where transformer architecture comes. There was a lot of evolution happening in 2016, 2017, and with this transformer I was excited to actually put it in production and build a product around this. Specifically, I was always excited about the idea of machines writing code. In 2017 I left and with my co-founder Alex Kdanov we started NEAR AI with the idea: how do we actually teach machines to code?
quotes: My team was working on question answering, machine translation, and as part of that, due to even requirements and latency for google.com, we were trying to figure out how to actually build a deep learning model that can consume lots of context and really reason about it without taking a ton of time to process that. That's where transformer architecture comes.

There was a lot of evolution happening in 2016, 2017, and with this transformer I was excited to actually put it in production and build a product around this. In 2017 I left and with my co-founder Alex Kdanov we started NEAR AI with the idea: how do we actually teach machines to code?

The response connects Polosukhin's enthusiasm for transformers to his ambition to teach machines to write code.

items.question: How do you assess the feasibility of what you were trying to build when you left Google in 2017 to teach machines to code?
items.object: The feasibility of teaching machines to code in 2017
items.answer:
Back then nobody thought what's happening right now is possible. What we were pitching was somewhere between science fiction and illusion. The reality is back then it wasn't possible. The compute wasn't there. The scale at which we know these models are needed wasn't there and wasn't studied very well.

On our side, what we're trying to do is get a lot more training data that is relevant to this problem, which is people writing some code for descriptions or writing descriptions for some code. We found a niche of people around the world who would do this for reasonably cheap. It was computer science students in developing countries. We built a crowdsourcing platform for computer science students where they can go and effectively practice their coding and get paid.

items.question: What made you decide that paying contributors to your coding-data platform required building NEAR Protocol?
items.object: Blockchain payments and the decision to build NEAR Protocol
items.answer:
The challenge we faced was the students were in China, Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia. In all of those countries there's some kind of problem with paying. In China people don't have bank accounts, they have WeChat Pay. In Ukraine, for example, you need to sell half of your dollars on arrival if it's in a foreign currency. Some countries, nothing worked. PayPal didn't work. Wise didn't work. So we started looking at blockchain as, hey, this global payment network people are talking about, we can just use it to pay people.

This was 2018. There was nothing that really matched our requirements. We're sending small amounts of money, microtransactions, and we didn't want to make it super complicated for them. There was nothing easy to use and actually cheap; transaction fees were in dollars. That's how we thought, okay, we should solve this problem. We talked with other people; other people have this as well, so we can solve this problem and go back to AI with that already in the pocket. That's how NEAR Protocol was born.

items.question: Why do you see user-owned AI as an important direction for the technology?
items.object: User-owned AI as a response to the centralization of AI
items.answer:
In 2022, 2023, as the resurgence of this and figuring out the scale of AI came in, we started with a renewed lens of the blockchain looking at it and seeing how can we contribute. Pretty quickly, as you work in blockchain you get indoctrinated by the value of user ownership, self ownership, self-sovereignty. It was pretty clear that the AI space changed. It went from open research, everybody contributing, the papers published, transformer code out for everybody to build on top, to everybody keeping a secret, things starting to close up. That leads to more centralization, monopolization of the technology, and in turn the monopoly we've seen before in other areas.

The example that I use is AOL. Imagine if internet was effectively run out of AOL. If you want to host a website you need to go to AOL and ask them to do this, and as a user you can only access through this. In the case of AI, because it's such a fundamental technology—it's intelligence as a technology—it's so much more dangerous. Internet is information, but this is the processing, the decision-making. The realization was that if we have only a handful of closed source, profit-driven companies dominating a space, we may end up in a 1984 type situation, where a company can effectively decide how everybody thinks, because that's how we process information, how we're going to see the world.

That's where this idea of user-owned AI was born: let's combine what we've been building on the blockchain side, user ownership and network effects of everybody contributing and participating, in comparison to centralized for-profit companies, and create an AI that actually is on the user side, on your side, not their side. There was a lot of open questions about how we actually do that. All the methods people use for privacy, for verifiability, are extremely expensive. There's homomorphic encryption, Z proofs, all of them have 10,000 to 100,000 times overhead. When we're talking about machine learning, which is already using all the compute possible, let's layer in two super compute intensive projects.

items.question: What do you find interesting about confidential computing in Nvidia and Intel hardware?
items.object: Confidential computing in Nvidia and Intel hardware
items.answer: We've been doing a lot of research, and the interesting thing that happened is the hardware. Nvidia hardware and Intel both, at a similar time, enabled this mode called confidential computing. This is inside the chips itself. You can enable it in such a way that even the owner of the hardware, of the compute, is not able to access what computation is happening inside, but whoever requested this compute can have a certificate saying that this data was run on this compute, let's say Docker, and this is the response.
quotes: We've been doing a lot of research, and the interesting thing that happened is the hardware. Nvidia hardware and Intel both, at a similar time, enabled this mode called confidential computing. This is inside the chips itself.

You can enable it in such a way that even the owner of the hardware, of the compute, is not able to access what computation is happening inside, but whoever requested this compute can have a certificate saying that this data was run on this compute, let's say Docker, and this is the response.

rubrics.text: The response explains that confidential computing on Nvidia and Intel chips can prevent even the hardware owner from accessing the computation occurring inside the chips.
The response explains that the compute requester can receive a certificate attesting that the returned result came from running the submitted data through the specified computation.

items.question: How do you see recent advances in confidential computing hardware changing what's possible for decentralized confidential machine learning?
items.object: Confidential computing hardware and decentralized confidential machine learning
items.answer: There was a lot of research and hardware over the years trying to do this, but historically it's been very low level. You needed to rewrite your programs in assembly, effectively, or C with special instructions. Intel in mid-2024 released on the new fifth-generation Xeons this new generation which allows you to exactly run just Docker. Similarly Nvidia enabled work with that specific mode where drivers inside can connect to Nvidia in the secure mode. That all came together effectively about a year ago. Since then, that gives us some components, but we still need the whole system. That's really what we're enabling. We call it decentralized confidential machine learning.

The response states that available confidential-computing hardware components do not by themselves constitute a complete decentralized confidential machine-learning system.

items.question: Why do you think confidentiality matters even for users who say they don't care about privacy?
items.object: Confidentiality and users' willingness to share data
items.answer: For the user, a lot of people are like, “I don't really care about privacy.” There's people who care about privacy, but still use all the products that take all their data. There are still some things that you're not going to trust. We don't normally walk around with a hot mic that records everything we say.

There are still some things that you're not going to trust. We don't normally walk around with a hot mic that records everything we say.

rubrics.text: The response observes that concern about privacy can coexist with using products that collect one's personal data.
The response states that even people who profess not to care about privacy have limits on the data collection they will trust.

items.question: How do you see confidentiality changing people's willingness to trust AI systems with their personal data?
items.object: Confidentiality and the threshold for trusting AI systems with personal data
items.answer: There's just so much context in your life that right now we're still not putting into these AI systems. Everybody's on a different spectrum. I, for example, don't trust my email and my calendar to maybe an AI company. Some people would, but then they wouldn't trust it with their medical data, or maybe they wouldn't trust it with their banking data. There's always a threshold where you get, “Maybe I shouldn't do that.” What we offer is effectively removing that threshold and saying, “Hey, actually it's all confidential, all end-to-end encrypted for you, and you can trust that there's no other single party—not developers, not operators of hardware, not model developers—able to access it.” It's as if it was local and potentially even better than local because you have additional security mechanisms.

items.question: How do you see secure enclaves addressing the privacy and control concerns around running AI models?
items.object: Secure enclaves for private AI inference
items.answer: A lot of people build their own clusters because they want to control everything. Obviously there's some efficiency from optimizations, but a lot of it is we want to literally have guards on the doors to make sure nobody can access. We're also solving that problem because of secure enclaves. You can encrypt the model weights and they only get decrypted inside the secure enclave, and user data is also private. You're bringing privacy from both sides: model developers don't need to deal with user data, they don't need to rent the hardware; it gets rented at the moment when users are using it. On the user side, users don't have access to the model but they also know their data is not going anywhere.

items.question: How do you understand the cloud's role in letting you use an AI model while keeping your data private?
items.object: The cloud as a middle layer for private AI processing
items.answer: So this cloud is the middle layer. As an end user, I'm contributing my data in some way because I want some processing on my data or to access intelligence, and the cloud can't access my data. Presumably the model provider can't access my data, but the model provider is providing the model into this cloud, and it can access my data and return some results back to me.

items.question: Why do you see training AI models on user data as a liability for model providers?
items.object: User data as a liability for AI model providers
items.answer: Imagine I'm a European, I'm in Lisbon right now, I use OpenAI. I'm assuming it's because they've just ignored it, and at one point there may be a challenge, but we're just not there yet.

items.object: User-data liability for smaller AI model developers
items.answer: So that's what I mean by liability. Maybe OpenAI has the money to pay their fine, similar to how Google and Facebook have paid billions of dollars in fines. But if you're a smaller model developer, this effectively can be existential.

items.question: Why do you think AI model development is transitioning away from user feedback?
items.object: The transition away from user feedback in AI model development
items.answer: I think the space is transitioning from user feedback. Let's use the DeepSeek example. When DeepSeek released their first model, which was at least at the time state-of-the-art from the open weight models, like our R1, it did not use the explicit user queries.

items.question: How do you see the balance shifting between curated supervision and ordinary user feedback in training AI models?
items.object: Curated supervision versus user feedback in AI model training
items.answer:
I think it's a combination of data labeling, indeed human, but you actually want very specific supervision and you want to control what feedback you get. Human labeling is its own space where there's a lot of know-how about how to do it properly, and we've been running that for years. There is synthetic data, there is verifiable math, physics, logic, coding, etc., which clearly improve reasoning as well.

Even if we're talking about shifting the vibe of the model, which is something usually credited to Claude versus OpenAI—the vibe is different—even that, you probably want more trained people to give feedback versus just relying on a very noisy signal that comes from users. Again, it's not fully transitioning to this, and it depends on the use cases. It's important to note, but the cost versus reward is shifting, and it's shifting faster than at least some people realize.

items.question: How do you weigh collecting data from product users against paying people to contribute training data?
items.object: Collecting user data versus paying for contributed training data
items.answer: Again, it depends. For some things, audio for example, it's great to have a bunch of audio from people that use your product, but then you may get in trouble. We've seen that happening. I think it's better to just pay people to contribute their audio and sign off the rights. It's pretty straightforward to do that. We have a project on NEAR running that. That's what I mean by the shift: how much we can collect data and how useful that is versus getting a bunch of user data and dealing with all the repercussions.

items.question: How do you think users should be treated when they opt in to contribute their data?
items.object: Opt-in user data contributions

items.question: How do you think model-specific tokens should reward people who contribute training data?
items.object: Model-specific tokens for rewarding training-data contributors
items.answer: We talked about this last year: effectively every model gets its own token, a way to distribute reward and value from the revenue, while also rewarding with this token. You can think of shares. Whoever contributed data gets a token of this model that will be trained on their data, and then the revenue is distributed to these token holders for the model's lifetime. We can run and guarantee those parameters as well.

items.question: How do you see private data contributions working in a model that compensates data providers?
items.object: Private data contributions with control over training and retrieval use
items.answer: I can say, “Hey, I want this data to be used in model training, but I don't want anyone to see it.” I can also say, “I want it to be used at inference time as part of your search retrieval index, but not at training.” You contribute it, it's payable. For example, for paid data, The New York Times can contribute their data fully privately into secure enclaves, and then it's going to be used at retrieval time, it's going to get recorded, and they're going to get paid for that. You get a lot of the pieces for free in this new model.

For example, for paid data, The New York Times can contribute their data fully privately into secure enclaves, and then it's going to be used at retrieval time, it's going to get recorded, and they're going to get paid for that. You get a lot of the pieces for free in this new model.

items.question: How do you think open-source AI development needs to change as open models catch up with closed models?
items.object: Open-source AI development and an open training process
items.answer:
I think I was trying to remember—it was February 2023, I was talking about, “Hey, open source is going to catch up.” The challenge with pure open source right now, and this is something we're solving, is I built the model, I released it, everybody's like, “Cool, here's stars on GitHub, stars on Hugging Face,” but then you don't make any money. It's not because of that; it also becomes less about open source and more about open weights. People keep the source so they can continue doing things. As a result we're wasting a lot of resources because everybody's redoing experiments. We don't know what people did to get to these results, so everybody needs to reproduce or poach the people who've done it.

The way we think about it is to reverse it, where you can have an open process of training. The data is either fully open or encrypted data that you can run over.

items.question: How do you see encrypted models running through DCML making open research and collaboration compatible with monetization?
items.object: Monetizing encrypted models through DCML while preserving open research and collaboration
items.answer:
You need to pay to access it in whatever, your model token or some other way, if you're planning to monetize differently. The resulting weights are also encrypted and only run in this DCML model. So I can monetize it; I can receive revenue from using it. I can say, “Compute cost is X. I want 20 cents per million tokens over that to go to the model developers and all the contributors.” You can reverse that and get actual open research and collaboration happening while monetizing the outcomes.

The benefit is you still get all the properties of open source. Everybody can use it. There's no way to stop using it. You can even run it on your hardware if you have modern Blackwell or Hopper and set it up in this central mode, and you can fine-tune it. You can do all those things on top.

items.question: How do you see privacy making personal AI appealing beyond the relatively small audience willing to pay for privacy itself?
items.object: Privacy as a way to make personal AI more useful
items.answer:
I don't think the issue is that there's never that audience. It's that it's relatively small. But the idea here is everybody's on a threshold of what they feel they would give to the model. The more you give, the better. We're getting to a stage where models are generally sufficiently intelligent, and it all becomes about context, context management, tool management, all the pieces. The idea we're very much going after is that because it's private, you can share a lot more with it. You'll add your email, calendar, medical data, financial data, crypto wallet, etc. It's able to manage your whole life, not just some aspects you were willing to share.

The first cohort that cares about privacy is our early adopters, who we target to enable this. As this becomes mature, it's appealing to more people because it's a better product and smarter, more intelligent product, not because the model is right away more intelligent, but because you have more context.

items.question: How do you expect a cloud where applications run on the user's side to create network effects around personal AI?
items.object: Network effects around private user data, specialized models, and applications
items.answer: Because of this open research process, what we're aiming for is to have people fine-tuning specialized models for specialized use cases. Because they have monetization embedded, they can invest effort, time, and compute to build interesting specialized models that may be better at financial use cases, healthcare, etc. All of them are available on your platform; they can compute over your data. Now that all your data is there, it's useful to other developers as well. If I'm building a notetaker, I can build one that takes all your data, listens to it all the time, sends it to my server, stores it on my server, but there's liability and it's a hurdle for everybody else to adopt it. Or I can build my app and deploy it into this cloud where it runs on your side and saves context in your data store. Your data store becomes more useful because it has all the notes, and your AI can read over those notes, so you don't need to merge things with Zapier and do all that. The idea is network effects: more context, more data, more applications building around the user. It starts with early adopters who care about privacy and layers on as more applications become available on this cloud.

items.question: How do you think about the trade-off between model-deployment flexibility and user security in your private AI environment?
items.object: Model-deployment flexibility and user security in the private AI environment
items.answer: We effectively run vLLM and a customized version of vLLM, so everything that is normally served already works. If you need something custom, you can also package your own Docker. That is less secure from a user side, but it's also available. The secure enclave ensures that there's no man-in-the-middle attack between vLLM, the model weights, and the customer data.

items.question: How do you think about making private model execution verifiable in NEAR’s infrastructure?
items.object: NEAR’s use of secure enclaves, on-chain verification, and multi-party computation for private model execution
items.answer:
You checkpoint your model weights on-chain: the hash of the model weights and the encrypted hash as well. The encrypted data is uploaded to decentralized storage. When somebody wants to run a model, they have an encrypted TLS connection directly into the secure enclave. That secure enclave gives you back the signed certificates that it runs in the secure enclave. You can verify them with our on-chain key management system.

We also have this concept called multi-party computation. The NEAR blockchain itself, part of our nodes, forms this multi-party computation network, which allows the secure enclave effectively to have its own private key to decrypt things. That's how all those pieces work together. If you encrypt something, it needs a key that is only known inside the secure enclave and nowhere else. The MPC network enables that. You encrypt locally, upload checkpoints, and when a user calls, they know the secure enclave will respond that this model hash was run on your data. Here is a signature by Nvidia, Intel, etc. You can also verify certificate provisioning.

items.question: Why do you see openness about how AI models are trained as important for trusting them?
items.object: Transparency in AI model training as a foundation for trust
items.answer: Especially as AI will be how we interface with computing, you ideally want to make sure there are no biases that are not represented with your view. I think there are a few components to improving trust in these models. I think it starts with the open process of how these models were trained, because there's this concept of sleeper agents. You can train things into the model so that at some point, under some conditions, it activates and behaves in a different way than normal. You can introduce vulnerabilities in the code into a coding tool based on some condition. I'm assuming if somebody wants to do a new Stuxnet, that's how they're going to do it. items.question: How do you think formal verification should give users guarantees when they invoke an AI system?
items.object: Invocation verification for software and AI systems
items.answer:
We're looking at formal verification. When we talk about software and AI systems, we're testing some use cases, some evals, maybe vibe testing, but we don't really have guarantees that the system will comply with some requirements. Formal verification is a way to achieve that, and it should be happening at the invocation side. As you call something, the example closer to blockchain is if you're putting money into something, you want to make sure you can get at least as much money back, that nobody will be able to steal your money, for example with a savings account. You want the guarantee when you put in your money; you want the proof at that time. We call it invocation verification.

Similarly, when you call an AI system, you can say, “You can access my email, but you cannot delete anything. You cannot leak anything. You cannot do this set of actions.” The system, the TE, the secure enclave that runs it, proves that the code inside complies with your requirements. This Docker hash complies with these requirements. Now you have not just proof of verifiability, but proof of specific preconditions. If it fails, if it doesn't match your preconditions, this doesn't execute.

items.question: Why do you see composable guarantees as essential when AI systems call other AI systems and tools?
items.object: Composable guarantees across interconnected AI systems and tools
items.answer: We need them, especially as things start to call each other. When you have one AI system calling another AI system, calling an MCP tool, calling another AI system, the idea is the properties are composable. If this service proves to you that it will work in this specific way when it calls other services, those services need to prove it as well, and if they don't, it's not able to call it. That's really important: it gives you this composable effect, which I think right now is the biggest problem. Imagine systems becoming more complex, all these AIs talking to each other, and we have no idea what they agree on doing and what they end up executing. That's going to be a fundamental system change, but it requires verifiability because you need something to guarantee the code inside is following these properties, some containerization that you can trust.
